sourceBindings.text: Arrange samples A, B and C separately with a clean tray, spray bottle, towels, ruler and recording sheet. Use the task protection selected by the trainer, including suitable gloves. Work only with the prepared safe mineral samples. If protection prevents reliable feel assessment, ask the trainer to resolve the method; do not simply remove required protection or use an unknown contaminated soil.

Write the sample ID first. Look at its colour, visible grains and clods, and note whether it is already moist. Keep this initial observation separate from the texture name you will decide later. A light, dark, red or grey appearance does not identify the texture on its own.

Take a small palm-sized portion. Remove stones, roots and other debris rather than testing a stone or root as though it were the fine soil. Keep the remaining bulk sample clean and separately labelled. Do not mix A with B or C.

The field feel test estimates texture. Practice and comparison with checked samples improve consistency, but the result is not an exact laboratory particle-size analysis or a nutrient test. You will use the observations in the following crop-reasoning step.

sourceBindings.text: Add water drop by drop and knead the soil. Break down soft clods with your fingers so the sample is uniformly moist. Aim for a workable, moist-putty consistency where the soil can be moulded if its texture allows it. Do not turn the whole test portion into a dripping slurry.

Try to form a ball. If it crumbles, first ask whether it is too dry. If it is overly wet, correct it with suitable dry material from the same sample and knead again. Recheck before interpreting the failure. Do not add clay from another sample to make a sandy sample stick.

If a correctly conditioned mineral sample still cannot remain in a ball, the decision guide leads towards sand. Record the non-formation instead of inventing a ribbon length. If it does hold a ball but will not form a ribbon, the guide leads towards loamy sand. These are different outcomes; 'no ribbon' alone is not enough to distinguish them.

A screen control that adds simulated water only represents an action. The number of clicks is not a measured moisture percentage. In the real task, judge the prepared sample and its behaviour; do not chase an invented universal target such as 50–75% moisture.

sourceBindings.text: If a ball forms, place it between thumb and forefinger. Gently press with the thumb and push soil upward into a strip of reasonably even width and thickness. Let the strip extend over the forefinger until it breaks under its own weight. Do not stretch it like dough or support a long strip with the other hand and call that its unsupported length.

Measure the ribbon length at breakage with the centimetre ruler, or clearly label an estimate. Record strength and consistency as well as the length. A picture of a ball is not evidence of a long ribbon. If an illustration asks you to compare lengths, it must show the ribbon and an appropriate scale.

The guide separates a weak ribbon shorter than 2.5 cm, an intermediate ribbon from 2.5 cm to under 5 cm, and a strong ribbon reaching 5 cm or more. These are field branches, not precise laboratory percentages of clay. Repeat borderline or inconsistent results and record uncertainty rather than forcing a sharp label from an approximate measurement.

Then take a small separate pinch, wet it more thoroughly and rub it to compare gritty and smooth sensations as the guide directs. This small wet pinch is the feel check; it is not permission to flood the main ribbon-test portion. Combine its feel with the ribbon branch.

sourceBindings.text: For a short ribbon below 2.5 cm, very gritty feel points towards sandy loam and very smooth feel towards silt loam. If neither grittiness nor smoothness dominates, the guide points towards loam. A short ribbon by itself does not establish loam.

For the intermediate branch, very gritty feel points towards sandy clay loam, very smooth feel towards silty clay loam, and neither sensation dominating towards clay loam. Do not label every 2.5–5 cm ribbon simply loam.

For a strong ribbon reaching 5 cm or longer, the corresponding branches are sandy clay, silty clay and clay. A long strong ribbon supports a clay-rich interpretation; the extra feel check helps choose the more specific class.

Use the decision guide consistently. If the sample does not behave clearly, record the observations, repeat the technique and discuss the uncertainty with the trainer. Sample letters and model answers are not measurements. A may be the sandy sample in one workshop and C in another.

sourceBindings.text: During the demonstration, the trainer says: 'I have written A and its initial colour. I am removing a small stone and a root. I add a little water, knead, and check whether the material holds together. It is not ready while it is dry inside or dripping outside.' Follow the order, not just the final texture name.

The trainer continues: 'Now I try the ball. If it holds, I press an even ribbon and let it break by itself. I record its length, then check the feel of a small wetter pinch. I follow both branches before writing a class. If it will not make a ball after conditioning, that is the result I record.' The demonstration must include a valid non-ribbon outcome as well as a ribbon-forming example.

Work in a group of three or four if directed, rotating tester, recorder and materials roles. Each learner still performs the full procedure on A, B and C and keeps attributable observations. Clean hands or gloves and the contact surface between samples so clay carried from one does not change the next sample's behaviour.

If learners disagree on the same sample, compare water addition, kneading, ribbon width, support and the recorded feel. Repeat consistently and discuss the evidence. Do not change a result just to match a table or another group. A five-minute reminder helps you finish recording; it does not justify skipping a sample or fabricating observations.

sourceBindings.text: For each sample, record initial colour, dry or moist state, gritty/smooth/sticky feel, ball outcome, ribbon outcome and length, whether the length was measured or estimated, the decision path and your texture conclusion. Record a repeat or uncertainty where needed. Keep original observations visible if you later revise the conclusion.

A worked sandy example may be light tan with coarse visible grains; a clay-rich example may be reddish-brown or dark grey and sticky; a loam example may be dark brown and feel mixed. These are possible appearances, not mandatory colours. Correct the classification from the actual behaviour, not from the example's sample letter.

Keep the crop-recommendation fields for the next step. The complete workshop asks for at least two justified candidates per sample. One of those also meets the original practical card's one-crop minimum. Testing texture does not on its own prove that either crop will suit the site.

Return or dispose of the samples as instructed, clean the surface and tools, remove protection appropriately and wash your hands. Rate your confidence and name a part you need to practise again. Confidence is useful feedback, but only observed individual work demonstrates the practical criteria.

For each sample, record initial colour, dry or moist state, gritty/smooth/sticky feel, ball outcome, ribbon outcome and length, whether the length was measured or estimated, the decision path and your texture conclusion. Record a repeat or uncertainty where needed. Keep original observations visible if you later revise the conclusion.

A worked sandy example may be light tan with coarse visible grains; a clay-rich example may be reddish-brown or dark grey and sticky; a loam example may be dark brown and feel mixed. These are possible appearances, not mandatory colours. Correct the classification from the actual behaviour, not from the example's sample letter.
